lines.v1: Developers have more help than ever. And less certainty about how to use it.
lines.v3: Alex asks an AI agent to move billing to a new payments system.
lines.v4: Minutes later, sixty-three files have changed.
lines.v5: Buried in file forty-one, the agent made a call nobody asked for.
lines.v7: We can see it. Alex can't.
lines.v8: Alex starts reading. Then the team's changes arrive for review.
lines.v9: It's more code than Alex can absorb.
lines.v10: And whatever ships, Alex is accountable for it.
lines.v12: Amid all the speculation, they're all left with one question.
lines.v14: With each new AI release, it comes back in a new form.
lines.v15: How much of my daily work should I hand to AI, and what must I still own?
lines.v16: So we went to developers in the trenches. Eight hundred and sixty of them, at a frontier tech company, Microsoft.
lines.v17: We asked how they wanted to integrate AI responsibly in their work, and where they resisted it, across the software lifecycle.
lines.v18: From their answers, we synthesized thirty-five developer-facing guidelines.
lines.v19: Across five kinds of software work: development, design and planning, quality and risk, infrastructure and operations, and meta-work.
lines.v21: A year later, as AI and developers' experiences kept evolving, we went wider.
lines.v22: Across companies and domains. Microsoft. GitHub. Pfizer.
lines.v23: Developers found the guidelines clear and relevant. And eighty-nine percent wanted to adopt them.
lines.v24: They described using AI to refine their craft and delegate work they could effectively verify, while demanding transparency and traceability, and keeping judgment and accountability for themselves.
lines.v25: Back to Alex. Take two. This time, with the guidelines.
lines.v26: Alex hands off the routine work, but demands a plan of action first.
lines.v27: Alex demands that the agent ask for clarification instead of acting on inferred context.
lines.v28: So the agent asks about large refunds. Alex gets to decide.
lines.v29: Alex also demands its work in self-contained pieces Alex can review, with its assumptions and sources in plain view.
lines.v30: Four small pull requests. Alex can read every one.
lines.v31: This time, Alex better understands what ships.
lines.v32: We offer these guidelines from developers in the trenches, to other developers in the trenches.
lines.v33: As a shared vocabulary for teams, and as skills for their agents: instructions an agent loads when a task calls for them.
lines.v34: Whether agents that follow them improve developers' work is still open. Try them, and tell us how it goes.
